title: Cell respiration
summary: How cells release energy from glucose and fatty acids to make ATP, how aerobic and anaerobic respiration differ, and (HL) the detailed stages from glycolysis to chemiosmosis.

keyterms.definition: Adenosine triphosphate: a nucleotide that distributes energy within cells; hydrolysis to ADP and phosphate releases energy for cell processes.
Controlled release of energy from carbon compounds such as glucose and fatty acids, used to produce ATP within the cell.
Cell respiration using oxygen; glucose is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and water with a large yield of ATP. Requires mitochondria.
Cell respiration without oxygen in the cytoplasm; glucose is partly broken down (to lactate in humans) with a small yield of ATP.
The product of anaerobic respiration in humans, formed from pyruvate; no carbon dioxide is produced.
Apparatus measuring respiration rate from oxygen uptake, with an alkali (e.g. soda lime) absorbing carbon dioxide so volume changes reflect oxygen use.
A hydrogen carrier; it accepts hydrogen (two electrons and a proton) when substrates are oxidised, becoming reduced NAD.
Loss of electrons or removal of hydrogen from a compound; in respiration, substrates are oxidised and NAD is reduced.
Stepwise conversion of glucose to two pyruvate in the cytoplasm: phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation and ATP formation; net yield 2 ATP and 2 reduced NAD.
Removal of carbon as carbon dioxide from a compound, occurring in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
Oxidation and decarboxylation of pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix, forming an acetyl group carried by coenzyme A (acetyl CoA).
Cyclical pathway in the matrix where acetyl groups are oxidised and decarboxylated, yielding CO2, ATP, reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
Carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons from reduced NAD, using the energy released to pump protons into the intermembrane space.
ATP synthesis driven by protons diffusing down their gradient through ATP synthase, which phosphorylates ADP.
Oxygen, which accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain and combines with protons to form water, allowing electron flow to continue.

questions.prompt: Which process does NOT directly use energy from ATP?
options: Active transport of ions across membranes
Synthesis of macromolecules such as proteins
Movement of chromosomes during mitosis
Diffusion of oxygen into a cell
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive: molecules move down their concentration gradient without ATP. Active transport, anabolism and movement (of whole cells or of components within them) all need ATP.

questions.statement: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy that can be used by the cell.
questions.explanation: Breaking off the terminal phosphate releases energy for cell processes. Energy from respiration is then needed to rebuild ATP from ADP and phosphate.

questions.text: Cell respiration should not be confused with ___, which is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with the environment.
questions.explanation: Cell respiration is a set of enzyme-catalysed reactions inside cells that produce ATP. Gas exchange is the diffusion of gases at a surface such as the alveoli.

questions.prompt: What are the principal substrates for cell respiration?
options: Glucose and fatty acids
Amino acids and nucleotides
ATP and ADP
Oxygen and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Glucose and fatty acids are the main carbon compounds oxidised in respiration. Proteins are used only when other substrates run out; oxygen is a reactant, not a substrate.

questions.statement: Cell respiration creates energy in the form of ATP.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created. Respiration releases energy stored in carbon compounds and transfers it to ATP.

questions.prompt: Why is ATP, rather than glucose, used to distribute energy within the cell?
options: ATP contains more energy per molecule than glucose
ATP can only be made in mitochondria
ATP is soluble, moves easily, and its hydrolysis releases a small, usable amount of energy
ATP is stored in large amounts in cells
questions.explanation: ATP releases energy in small, manageable amounts in a single reaction, and it diffuses easily to where it is needed. Cells hold little ATP and continuously regenerate it.

questions.text: ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and ___, releasing energy.
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis removes the third phosphate group from ATP. Re-attaching the phosphate (phosphorylation of ADP) requires energy from respiration.

questions.prompt: Match each life process to an example that uses ATP.

pairs.right: Pumping ions against a concentration gradient

questions.explanation: ATP supplies energy for active transport across membranes, synthesis of macromolecules and movement of whole cells or of components within cells.

questions.prompt: Put the ATP–ADP cycle in order, starting from ADP.
items: ADP and phosphate are present in the cell
Energy from cell respiration is used to join them
ATP moves to a site where energy is needed
ATP is hydrolysed, releasing energy and forming ADP and phosphate
questions.explanation: ATP is continuously recycled: respiration rebuilds it from ADP and phosphate, and hydrolysis at the site of use releases energy and regenerates ADP.

questions.prompt: What is ATP chemically?
options: A lipid with three fatty acids
A nucleotide with adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
A polysaccharide of glucose units
An amino acid with three phosphate groups
questions.explanation: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide: the base adenine, the sugar ribose and a chain of three phosphate groups.

questions.prompt: Match each feature to the correct description for humans.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration happens entirely in the cytoplasm and forms lactate; aerobic respiration starts in the cytoplasm and is completed in mitochondria, producing CO2 and water.

questions.statement: Anaerobic respiration in human muscle produces carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: In humans, anaerobic respiration converts glucose to lactate only; no CO2 is released. Yeast is different: it produces ethanol and CO2.

questions.text: Word equation for anaerobic respiration in humans: glucose → ___
questions.explanation: Human anaerobic respiration produces lactate. Ethanol and CO2 are the products in yeast; CO2 and water are the products of aerobic respiration.

questions.text: Word equation for aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + ___
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose to carbon dioxide and water. ATP is produced, but it is not written as a product in the word equation.

questions.statement: Mitochondria are needed for anaerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration takes place entirely in the cytoplasm. Only aerobic respiration needs mitochondria.

questions.prompt: When do human muscle cells use anaerobic respiration?
options: Only when glucose is unavailable
When oxygen supply cannot meet demand, e.g. during short bursts of vigorous exercise
Only during sleep
Whenever ATP is needed
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration gives a rapid but small supply of ATP when oxygen is insufficient, such as during sprinting; lactate builds up and is removed later.

questions.prompt: Compare the ATP yield per glucose of aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
options: Both produce about the same amount
Anaerobic produces more ATP because it is faster
Aerobic produces much more ATP because glucose is fully oxidised
Neither produces ATP directly
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration yields far more ATP per glucose (around 30) than anaerobic respiration (2), because energy in lactate is not released.

questions.prompt: In a respirometer containing germinating seeds and soda lime, why does the coloured liquid move towards the seeds?
options: Oxygen is used, and the CO2 released is absorbed by the soda lime, so gas volume decreases
The seeds release oxygen during respiration
The soda lime releases carbon dioxide
The temperature inside the tube rises
questions.explanation: Soda lime (or KOH) absorbs CO2, so the only volume change is oxygen uptake. As oxygen is used, pressure falls and the liquid moves towards the organisms.

questions.prompt: 5 g of germinating seeds absorbed 1.0 cm³ of oxygen in 10 minutes. What was their rate of respiration?
options: 0.5 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹
2.0 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹
0.1 cm³ min⁻¹ for the whole sample, ignoring mass
0.02 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹
questions.explanation: Rate = 1.0 cm³ ÷ 10 min ÷ 5 g = 0.02 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹. Dividing by mass allows samples of different size to be compared.

questions.prompt: In a respirometer experiment testing the effect of temperature on respiration of seeds, which variable must be controlled?
options: Temperature of the water bath
Mass of seeds used
Distance moved by the liquid
Rate of oxygen uptake
questions.explanation: Temperature is the independent variable and oxygen uptake (distance moved) is the dependent variable. Mass of seeds must be kept constant, along with seed type and time.

questions.prompt: What is the role of NAD in cell respiration?
options: It is the terminal electron acceptor
It phosphorylates ADP to ATP
It accepts hydrogen removed when substrates are oxidised, becoming reduced NAD
It removes carbon dioxide from pyruvate
questions.explanation: Oxidation is the removal of hydrogen (or electrons). NAD carries the hydrogen as reduced NAD, mainly to the electron transport chain.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of glycolysis in order.
items: Oxidation of triose phosphate, reducing NAD
Formation of 4 ATP and two pyruvate
questions.explanation: Glucose is first phosphorylated (using 2 ATP), split into two 3C molecules, oxidised (2 NAD reduced), and then 4 ATP are formed, a net gain of 2 ATP.

questions.statement: Glycolysis needs oxygen to take place.
questions.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration; it needs NAD, not oxygen.

questions.prompt: Why is pyruvate converted to lactate in anaerobic respiration?
options: To release a large amount of extra ATP
To produce carbon dioxide
To store energy for later
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, reduced NAD cannot be oxidised by the electron transport chain. Reducing pyruvate to lactate oxidises NAD, so glycolysis can continue to make 2 ATP.

questions.text: In yeast, anaerobic respiration converts pyruvate to ethanol and ___; this gas makes bread dough rise.
questions.explanation: Yeast regenerates NAD by converting pyruvate to ethanol and CO2. In baking the CO2 makes dough rise; in brewing the ethanol is the useful product.

questions.prompt: What happens in the link reaction?
options: Glucose is split into two pyruvate
Pyruvate is oxidised and decarboxylated, and the acetyl group is carried by coenzyme A
Acetyl groups combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate
Protons flow through ATP synthase
questions.explanation: In the matrix, pyruvate loses CO2 (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD); the remaining acetyl group is attached to coenzyme A.

questions.prompt: Match each stage to its products.

pairs.right: Acetyl CoA, CO2 and reduced NAD
CO2, ATP, reduced NAD and reduced FAD
Proton gradient across the inner membrane

questions.explanation: Each stage oxidises its substrate; most of the energy ends up in reduced NAD, which feeds the electron transport chain to build a proton gradient for ATP synthesis.

questions.text: In the Krebs cycle, an acetyl group (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form ___ (6C).
questions.explanation: Citrate is then oxidised and decarboxylated twice, releasing 2 CO2 and regenerating oxaloacetate, which makes the pathway cyclical.

questions.prompt: Put the events of oxidative phosphorylation in order.
items: Reduced NAD donates electrons to the electron transport chain
Electrons pass along carriers, releasing energy
Energy is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space
Protons diffuse back to the matrix through ATP synthase
ATP synthase phosphorylates ADP to ATP
Oxygen accepts electrons and protons, forming water
questions.explanation: Electron flow builds a proton gradient across the inner membrane; chemiosmosis through ATP synthase makes ATP, and oxygen removes electrons at the end so flow can continue.

questions.statement: Oxygen acts as the terminal electron acceptor, combining with electrons and protons to form water.
questions.explanation: By removing electrons and protons at the end of the chain, oxygen keeps electrons flowing. Without oxygen the chain stops and so does chemiosmotic ATP production.

questions.prompt: Why can lipids be used as a respiratory substrate only in aerobic respiration?
options: Fatty acids are broken into 2C acetyl groups that enter via acetyl CoA, bypassing glycolysis
Lipids are too large to enter cells
Lipids contain less energy per gram than carbohydrates
Lipids are converted to lactate
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are broken into acetyl groups that enter the Krebs cycle, which needs oxygen to regenerate NAD. Only carbohydrates go through glycolysis, the anaerobic stage. Lipids give more energy per gram.

questions.prompt: During chemiosmosis in mitochondria, in which direction do protons flow through ATP synthase?
options: From the matrix to the intermembrane space
From the cytoplasm to the matrix
From the intermembrane space to the matrix
From the matrix to the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space; they diffuse back down their gradient into the matrix through ATP synthase, driving ATP synthesis.
